units: still water fills the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds
its surface was clear before and now carries a greenish film
lasting heat speeds up the loss of water to evaporation
the dissolved minerals grow denser in what is left
the ground nearby dries out and splits into brittle pieces
plants rotting at the bottom give off a foul smell
the water insects disappear from the place
the birds that fed there quit the shore
the spring downhill barely supplies the growing plots any water
the growers bore deeper wells and pull the buried water lower
text: Still water lies in the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds. It ran clear once; now a greenish film sits across it and the wind barely creases the surface. Long stretches of heat are the first cause: the water leaves faster as vapor, and the minerals dissolved in it grow denser in whatever is left behind. Around the rim the ground bakes and splits into brittle plates that crumble underfoot. With nothing to stir it, the plant matter rots down below, and the smell that rises off the hollow turns the stomach. The water insects go first. The birds that used to feed on them quit the shore altogether. Farther downhill, the spring that once soaked the growing plots barely wets the soil now. So the growers bore deeper wells, and each one they sink pulls the buried water lower. Each drying spell sets up a harder one behind it.

units: the streets overheat because they are paved with asphalt and concrete
the air there turns hard to breathe as soon as the sun hits
heat related collapses are becoming more frequent
air conditioning is offered as the answer to the problem
an air conditioner throws outside the heat it pulls from inside
that equipment eats a huge amount of power
the writer proposes planting thick trees along the busy streets
he proposes making schoolyards soak up rain and laying pale surfaces
he calls for water where people stand and wait
he claims these measures need no untried technology but a budget
text: Let us be blunt for a second. Our streets bake because we paved them over with asphalt and concrete. The moment the sun hits, the air turns thick and hard to breathe, and then we act surprised that people keep going down in the heat. Air conditioning, we are told, is the fix. It fixes nothing. It shoves outdoors the very heat it pulls from indoors, and it eats power at a rate nobody wants to look at. There is a way out, and none of it is clever. Line the busy streets with trees thick enough to throw real shade. Break up the schoolyards so the rain soaks in. Swap black paving for pale surfaces that bounce the light back. Put water where people stand and wait. Not one of those waits on an invention nobody has made yet. They wait on a budget. Comfort is not something you cool. It is something you plant.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running a measuring station climbs weekly to a ring of rock walls
her predecessor logged ice thickness by hand
she now receives readings sent up automatically by sensors
the ice was once hard and bluish underfoot
the surface today is soft and gives under crampons
the glacier snout was once a clean edge and is now a thinned tongue
crumbling gravel streaks that tongue
she also watches two facing slopes of the same range
the slope that takes the sun loses its ice far faster than the other
she finds that gap more telling than an overall average figure
text: Once a week the woman who runs a measuring station hikes up to a ring of rock walls to take the readings off her instruments. The job is the one her predecessor held, but almost nothing about it has stayed put. He wrote ice thickness into a notebook by hand. She opens a screen and finds the readings waiting, sent up by sensors on their own. He walked on a hard bluish crust. She crosses a soft skin that gives under her crampons. Where his notes described a clean wall of ice at the snout, hers describe a thin tongue streaked with gravel that crumbles at a touch. She watches two facing slopes of the same range as well. The one that takes the sun head on gives up its ice far faster than the shaded one. That gap, she says, teaches her more than any average figure for the glacier as a whole.

units: the review covers a set of photographs devoted to drought
the first part shows split ground covered with whitish crust
the second part shows horizons veiled by heat
a third part gathers emptied riverbeds and abandoned watering equipment
the last part shows the people who stayed on
the reviewer calls that last part the finest
the whole set avoids complaint and moral lessons
the pictures are hung so that each one pulls you into the next
the reviewer holds that the quiet in the frames carries more weight than an argument
text: Seldom has a set of photographs handled drought with so light a hand. The opening sequence stays low, on the ground itself: clay split into plates, a chalky crust, pale dust that lifts at the smallest breath of wind. The next group leaves the earth for the air, where heat smears the far edge of things and the horizon dissolves into haze. A third gathers what the water left behind, riverbeds paved with stone, dry basins, watering hose coiled and forgotten like dead root. The last group, and the finest, turns to the people who stayed: dusty hands, weathered faces, eyes tipped up toward the sky. Nothing here complains and nothing preaches. The pictures are hung so that each one pulls you into the next, and the quiet inside those frames carries more weight than any argument could.

units: the writer sends word from a measuring post to describe a repair
he opened the case at the start of the week
a mineral crust covered the temperature probe and skewed the readings
he cleaned that probe in an acid bath while watching the time
he then put the unit back together and checked the gasket seal
the curve sat a fixed step off once the post restarted
so he recalibrated the unit against a reference probe
he cleaned the dirt covered solar panel and the charging voltage climbed back
the readings have come in without a break ever since
he invites the person he writes to over to see the monitoring board now in place
text: Writing from the measuring post, as promised, to tell you how the repair on the sensor turned out. I took the case apart at the start of the week and found the temperature probe under a hard mineral crust that was skewing every reading. I soaked it in an acid bath and stood over it with a timer, since the stuff chews through metal if you forget it. Next morning I put the unit back together and checked the gasket for a tight seal. Transmission picked up again, but the curve sat a fixed step off the true value, so I recalibrated against the reference probe. The day after that, I wiped the solar panel, gray with dust, and the charging voltage climbed right back. Nothing has dropped out of the record since. Come by the post whenever you like and take a look at the monitoring board now running.

units: a common question concerns the damp spreading through the walls of older housing
that damp comes from groundwater rising under the foundations
harder rain falling closer together feeds that rise
packed downpours saturate compacted soil that takes in nothing
the water then heads for the cellars
a waterproof coating seals the damp inside the masonry
masonry sealed that way turns friable and sheds in patches
specialists advise drainage around the building
they also advise renders that breathe and open ground nearby that takes water in
the answer on cost states that acting late comes to more
text: A question comes up at nearly every public meeting: where does the damp climbing the walls of older housing come from? It comes from groundwater rising under the foundations, and that rise is fed by rain that now falls harder and closer together. A second question follows: what has any of this to do with the climate? Downpours packed into an hour saturate compacted soil that takes in nothing at all, and the water goes looking for the cellars. Third question: is a waterproof coating not enough? It is not. Such a coating seals the moisture inside the masonry, which turns friable and sheds in patches. What is advised instead? Drainage around the building, renders that let a wall breathe, and open ground alongside that takes water in. The last question turns on cost, and the answer is blunt: waiting comes to more.

units: a fisherman tells an engineer the water has smelled wrong since the cold season
a brown scum clings to the stones on the bed
the smell sharpens when the level of the river drops
the engineer explains that a sewer line upstream spills over during storms
the fisherman objects that the trouble has run through too many seasons
the engineer also names the runoff from an animal operation on the plateau
the plan calls for a holding basin upstream
it also calls for a thick strip of planting along the banks
steady checks on what gets released are scheduled
the engineer says the insects coming back will signal the change
text: On the bank, a fisherman tells the engineer sent out to look into it that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season. She asks whether the color changed as well. He points to a brown scum stuck on the stones of the bed and says the stench climbs as soon as the level drops. She explains that a sewer line upstream spills over whenever a storm runs past what the pipes can hold. He is not satisfied: the trouble has run through too many seasons to hang on a few storms. She grants him that, and brings up the animal operation on the plateau, whose runoff drains down toward the bed. Then she lays out the plan, a holding basin upstream, a thick strip of planting along both banks, steady checks on what gets released. He asks when the water will run clear. The insects, she says, will tell him first.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in one valley wood was once burned for every purpose
the air smelled of smoke and the walls went black with soot
people took that state of affairs for granted
a dark fuel was then cut out of the rock
the energy yield rose sharply
workshops spread and the sky over the working valleys hazed over
the real turning point lies in the change of scale
a burned forest can grow back over generations
carbon drawn from a buried seam cannot be put back there
the old fires lived off what grew around them while the later ones drew on a store
text: Picture a valley where wood went into every fire, from the supper pot to the forge. The air smelled of smoke, the walls went black, and nobody thought twice about it. Set that beside what came after, once people started cutting into rock for a dark fuel. The heat you got out of a single load of it jumped. Workshops spread. The sky over the working valleys hung hazy from dawn to dusk. The real break, though, was one of scale. Burn a forest and it comes back, given enough generations of patience. Burn a seam out of the ground and the carbon it held has nowhere to go back to. The old fires lived off what grew around them, while the ones that followed drew down a store. Watch nothing but the flame and you will miss the difference. It shows only when you look at what feeds the flame.

units: three mechanisms account for the changes in the oceans
the first mechanism has to do with the heat the water soaks up
warmed water swells and raises the level with no ice melting
the second mechanism is chemical and comes from dissolved carbon dioxide
water turned acidic works away at shells and chalky skeletons
the third mechanism concerns the mixing of the water layers
the surface layer mixes less with the layers beneath it
that lid keeps nutrients from below away from the plankton
the three mechanisms feed one another
a sea with less life in it draws down less carbon
text: Three mechanisms are enough to account for what is happening to the oceans. The first is heat. Seawater soaks up a huge share of the warmth building up, and warm water swells, so the level climbs even where no ice has melted at all. The second is chemistry. As the sea takes in more carbon dioxide it turns slightly corrosive, and it works away at the shells and the chalky skeletons that shellfish and corals build for themselves. The third is stirring. A warmer surface layer mixes less readily with the cold water beneath it, and that lid keeps nutrients from rising, which leaves the plankton hungry. Each one bites on its own, and together they bite harder. Warmer, more acidic, more layered water carries less life, and a sea with less life in it draws down less carbon than before.

units: the keeper of a mountain refuge barred her shutters before the sky changed
a warm breath came down from the pass in the middle of the afternoon
a curtain loaded with sand then moved up the trail
sand settled even on the tables
the keeper knew the wind had carried that dust from dry country far off
rain stained the color of ochre fell at nightfall
that rain left hardened streaks on the windows
the snow on the nearby glacier had turned rust red by morning
that snow melted faster than the keeper had ever watched snow go
she wrote the event into her log without expecting it to happen again
text: The woman who kept the mountain refuge had barred her shutters before the sky gave any sign. Around the middle of the afternoon a warm breath slid down from the pass, close and heavy. Then the whole slope went blurred and dim. A curtain of sand came up the trail, and grit settled everywhere, even along the tabletops inside. She knew the wind for what it was: it had carried that dust off dry country far beyond the ridgelines. The rain came at dusk, thick and stained the color of ochre, and it dried on the windows in hard streaks. By morning the snow on the glacier below was no longer white but rust red, and it melted while she stood watching, faster than she had ever seen snow go. She wrote the whole of it down in her log. It did not once occur to her that it would happen again.
